events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) in Portland, Oregon will open two new exhibitions in its Front and Center Galleries this August. tende·r·eprisal // futu·re·prise, a group exhibition of bronze works created by multiple artists through a collaborative process led by elijah jamal asani, will be featured in the Front Gallery. In the Center Gallery, large-scale wood sculptures by Philip A. Robinson Jr. will be paired with functional and sculptural ceramic works by Swapna Mukhopadhyay. Both exhibitions run August 7–September 12, 2026, with a joint reception on Thursday, August 20, from 6 to 8 p.m. elijah jamal asani, a Nigerian-American artist, convened an intergenerational group of regional Black artists to create a collection of contemporary bronze artifacts. Their work was made in response to the historic theft of the Benin Bronzes. “Dating back to the 13th century, artists from the Kingdom of Benin, which is in modern-day southern Nigeria, cast bronze into sacred altar pieces and vessels of ancestral memory,” says asani. “However, in 1897, thousands of these bronze artifacts were looted by British forces.” They have yet to be repatriated. As an act of “selfdetermined restitution,” asani worked with other Black artists to create new bronzes. MAC is honored to exhibit eleven of these sculptures, created by Adriene Cruz, Midnite Seed Abioto, Intisar Abioto, Hanifah Abioto, Vaughn Kimmons, Turiya Raiah, Nyasiah Calixte, Lea Dry, Hannah Dry, Nawens Dry, and elijah jamal asani. Swapna Mukhopadhyay creates functional and sculptural porcelain works, all hand built. “The combination of aesthetics and functionality in handmade folk artifacts has always fascinated me,” she says. “My grandmother made traditional Bengali quilts (kanthas) and wove mats for sitting on the floor (asanas). I now realize how deeply I was influenced by watching her work.” Delicate drawn elements adorn many of her ceramic surfaces, and several recent works incorporate textiles and found objects. Mukhopadhyay describes her process as “improvising around what’s available,” informed by her longtime study of ethnomathematics. A retired PSU professor, she sees mathematics as inherent to creative practice and creative expression as integral to daily life across many cultures. Her ceramic pieces are often small in scale and characterized by what she calls their “putting togetherness.” Philip A. Robinson Jr. is a sculptor and conceptual artist whose work has been exhibited nationally and internationally. Working primarily in wood and metal, Robinson creates large-scale figurative and patterned works that explore memory, structure, and identity. “My practice examines structure as a living system—how materials carry memory, how patterns encode history, and how built environments shape identity,” he explains. “Whether in wood or steel, I am asking how structure holds memory—and how we locate ourselves within it.” The exhibition will include pieces from several bodies of work, including a 42” x 61” sculpture from Welcome In, which examines belonging, and several works from The House of Regina, which honor the legacy of his late mother, Dr. Regina Arnold. Robinson holds a BFA in Studio Art from Skidmore College and an MFA in Sculpture from the Mason Gross School of the Arts at Rutgers University. The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. The galleries are free and open to the public during these hours. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org

events.summary: Camp overview Ignite your passion for music in this five-day DJ camp designed for ages 11–14. Guided by Portland-based DJ Ambush, this hands-on program introduces campers to the creative and technical skills behind DJing: from foundational concepts to performance-ready techniques in a supportive, collaborative environment. Throughout the week, campers will gain hands-on experience with professional DJ equipment, learning how mixers, controllers, and software work together. They’ll explore music fundamentals, including rhythm, tempo, and song structure to better understand how to build engaging playlists and mixes. Working individually and in small groups, campers will develop beatmatching, mixing, and transition techniques while practicing creative problem-solving and teamwork. They’ll learn how DJs shape mood and tell a story through sound as they curate their own party-ready sets. The camp concludes with a celebratory DJ showcase, where campers share their mixes with friends and family, highlighting their creativity, confidence, and newly developed DJ skills. This camp is ideal for music-loving middle schoolers eager to explore performance, collaboration, and the art of mixing music. sold out – waitlist only About the teaching artist With a music career spanning over 30 years, DJ Ambush has worn many hats—DJ, Event Producer, Art Curator, Podcaster, Radio Personality, Organizer, and Host. Those talents have taken him up and down the East Coast \(where he’s from\) and have found him a home in Portland, Oregon. He’s driven by a desire to connect with the community across all intersections, and a passion to see people thriving and enjoying themselves.

events.summary: PDX CONTEMPORARY ART is pleased to present our summer group show Mixed Flock: 30 Years, marking the celebration of the gallery’s thirtieth anniversary. Mixed Flock comes from the idea of different species of birds gathering together for a variety of reasons including safety, cooperation, and community. In talking with wildlife scientist Derek Craighead about mixed flocks, Craighead suggested humans underestimate the sociability of animals, that wild animals will gather to be social, for fun, and for company. That’s worthwhile! For thirty years, PDX artist’s have been a wonderful mixed flock with each artist having their own way of seeing the world and approaching their art-making. Now is an important time to highlight and strengthen mixed flocks. Our country is a mixed flock, the “melting pot”, where diverse peoples, cultures, and ways exist together and we are better for it. This show is a celebration of the gallery’s many and varied artists, supporters, and collectors who make up our flock. Mixed Flock: 30 Years features work from represented and invited artists including: Anna Gray + Ryan Wilson Pauslen, Nick Blosser, Iván Carmona, Marjorie Dial, Amjad Faur, Bean Finneran, Jacques Flechemueller, Ellen George, Johannes GiararVictoria Haven, Elizabeth Knight, Justin L’Amie, Alma Allen, James Lavadour, Terran Last Gun, Nathan William Lambdin, Nancy Lorenz, Kristen Miller, Wes Mills, Jeffry Mitchell, Megan Murphy, Jenene Nagy, Ido Radon, Georgina Reskala, Joe Rudko, Tad Savinar, Susan Seubert, Adam Sorensen, Barbara Stafford, Storm Tharp, Gus Van Sant, Nell Warren, Heather Watkins, Marie Watt, and Yamamoto Masao.
events.title: Mixed Flock: 30 Years

Woven Light showcases the illuminated washi sculptures of Yuri Kinoshita, a Seattle-based artist who artfully crafts floating landscapes of light through her sculptural lamps that bridge the art and design world. Guests who visit the Calvin and Mayho Tanabe Gallery will see that through carefully hand-woven and sculpted washi (Japanese handmade paper made from plant fibers), soft light and shadow inspire a magical sense of place, evoking the unique environment of the Pacific Northwest. More than artwork, Kinoshita’s works are experiences that transport the viewer into a warm world of light through both works that evoke natural forms and abstracted shapes that inspire contemplation.

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Last Thursday Artist Reception: July 30, 6 to 9pm Show Dates: July 30 thru August 24, 11am to 7pm Immersive Worlds: Cities, Castles and Countrysides Explore the many worlds we inhabit, real and fantastical. Curated by North Pole Artist Max LaZebnik, this exhibition draws deeply from North Pole Studio’s archive to present a compelling selection of works that examine the spaces, landscapes, and communities that shape our sense of belonging. Moving between urban centers, fantastical structures, and rural environments, the featured works invite viewers to consider how meaning is constructed through place. North Pole Studio supports careers in the arts and exists to increase opportunities for artists with autism and intellectual/developmental disabilities to thrive as active members of the arts community. It fosters self-determination and facilitates meaningful connections through total engagement in the arts. Alberta Street Gallery is a cooperative gallery of 30 local artists in the heart of the Alberta Arts District in Northeast Portland. In addition to our members’ art, we mount monthly shows that begin on the “Last Thursday” of every month. Our front windows feature new work by two of our member artists, and we curate group shows in Lavaun's Community Gallery, a special exhibition space inside the gallery named for and made possible by gallery member Lavaun Benavidez Heaster, a legally blind collage artist who died in 2020.
events.title: Immersive Worlds: Cities, Castles and Countrysides

Together, their work explores the transformation of the natural world through elemental materials and traditional craftsmanship. Rooted in botanical forms and natural processes, both artists celebrate the enduring beauty found within growth, decay, and renewal. Their work reveals the quiet magic of nature translated through paint and metal.

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Where Do Geese Fly at Night?, San Francisco–based artist Lindsay Stripling's debut solo exhibition with the gallery. Through luminous watercolor paintings, Stripling creates dreamlike worlds where memory, intuition, and the rhythms of the natural world converge. Her imagined landscapes and nature-infused portraits blur the boundaries between observation and imagination, inviting viewers into spaces where storytelling becomes a means of navigating identity, belonging, and transformation. Rooted in experimentation, texture, and play, Stripling's practice embraces watercolor as both a precise and unpredictable medium. Layers of transparent color accumulate into richly atmospheric compositions that evoke fleeting memories, quiet psychological states, and the mysterious logic of dreams. Plants, animals, and human figures coexist in environments that feel at once deeply familiar and gently surreal, suggesting a world in which the human experience is inseparable from the more-than-human landscape. Throughout Where Do Geese Fly at Night?, Stripling explores themes of nature, time, community, psychology, and personal mythology. Rather than offering fixed narratives, her paintings unfold as open-ended visual poems, encouraging viewers to project their own memories and emotional landscapes into the work. Each composition balances meticulous craftsmanship with a spirit of curiosity, revealing beauty in uncertainty and wonder in the everyday. The exhibition's title poses a deceptively simple question, one that gestures toward the unseen journeys taking place beyond the limits of perception. Like migratory paths traced through darkness, Stripling's paintings invite contemplation of the invisible forces that shape our relationships with ourselves, one another, and the natural world. Lindsay Stripling is a San Francisco–based painter, illustrator, and educator. Working primarily in watercolor, she explores the intersections of storytelling, memory, dreams, and ecology through richly layered paintings that combine intimate portraiture with expansive natural imagery. Where Do Geese Fly at Night? marks her first solo exhibition with Chefas Projects.
events.title: LINDSAY STRIPLING | WHERE DO GEESE FLY AT NIGHT?

events.summary: Chefas Projects is delighted to welcome back sculptor Jessie Weitzel Le Grand for her fourth exhibition with the gallery entitled Astral Accessories. Communication arrives fractured: as static, interference, intuition, and half-remembered technologies that once promised connection. In Astral Accessories, Portland-based artist Jessie Weitzel Le Grand presents a new body of sculptural work that imagines obsolete technological devices as enigmatic relics from alternate realities. Equal parts artifact, machine, and living organism, the sculptures transform familiar forms into mysterious conduits for uncertainty, speculation, and wonder. Drawing on the visual language of outdated communications technology, the exhibition considers what remains when systems of transmission fail or become obsolete. Unmanageable and invisible, signals continue to pass through space, whirring beyond perception, like sirens too quiet to hear. Meaning emerges imperfectly through noise, distortion, and interruption, where messages are received as static, interference, and fragmented memory rather than clear transmission. Rather than offering resolution, Astral Accessories embraces ambiguity. The works suggest speculative tools for communicating across impossible distances: between worlds, across time, or with forms of intelligence that remain just beyond comprehension. Suspended between archaeology and science fiction, the sculptures ask viewers to reconsider the objects that mediate our relationships with technology, memory, and the unknown. Utilizing an eclectic array of materials, including ceramics, thermoplastic, flashe paint, and even materials used in fly tying, Weitzel Le Grand blurs the boundaries between art, artifact, and technology. Interested in exploring how we perceive reality and questioning the certainty of what we see, she embeds natural elements such as orchids, moths, and fragments of coral within computer motherboards, rotary telephones, and other obsolete technologies in disorienting, exuberant configurations. By reimagining these nostalgic devices in playful yet unfamiliar ways, she encourages viewers to question their function and invent their own narratives around the mysterious systems they seem to inhabit. By transforming obsolete technologies into uncanny relics, Weitzel Le Grand creates a landscape where the familiar becomes strange and failed technologies become vessels for new forms of connection. Jessie Weitzel Le Grand (b. 1987) was born and raised in Portland, Oregon, where she continues to live and work. She received a BFA from the Pacific Northwest College of Art and an MAT from Marylhurst University. Her work has recently been exhibited at Galerie Lefebvre & Fils (Paris, France), Outback Arthouse (Los Angeles, California), Oregon Contemporary (Portland, Oregon), and as part of Lazy Oaf's Take A Break exhibition (London, United Kingdom). She is the co-founder of carnation Contemporary, a collective of emerging and mid-career artists from the Pacific Northwest championing critical contemporary art, and Well Well Projects, an artist-member gallery in Portland's Kenton neighborhood. In 2025, she was featured in Create! Magazine Issue #49 and is currently represented by Chefas Projects.
events.title: JESSIE WEITZEL LE GRAND | ASTRAL ACCESSORIES

events.summary: This summer, a multi-sensory art experience called Shifting Realities will take over Porsche Studio Portland for a creative journey produced by artists from Portland and across the country. The space turns into a living canvas where you don’t just observe the work, you become part of it. Across multiple interactive environments, you’ll see sound take physical form, design in real time using light and gesture, and step into spaces that respond to your movement, energy, and input. From large-scale visual installations to hands-on creative moments and a multisensory tasting experience, each part of the experience is designed to blur the line between artist and audience. Guests move through the experience in timed groups, progressing together through each space while still having room to explore and interact along the way. Running June 4 through August 31, Shifting Realities is a 100 minute limited-run installation that’s built for all ages and occasions. Tickets start at $39 ($41.34 incl. fees), with reduced pricing for kids and options for VIP, private, and group bookings.

events.summary: Japanese guitarist and singer Hiroya Tsukamoto leads the next Portland Folkmusic Society's Global Folksong Workshop, Tsukamoto, who grew up in Kyoto, Japan, and lives in New York, is best known for his superb guitar playing -- among his distinctions is taking second place at the International Fingerstyle Guitar Championship both in 2018 and 2022. All ages $10 adv/$12 door. For this event Tsukamoto will focus on singing, and teaching participants to sing, a couple Japanese folk songs. “One is a traditional folk song called ‘Asadoya Yunta’ from Okinawa, Southern part of Japan,” Tsukamoto explained. ”Prior to Japan, Okinawa was an kingdom called Ryukyu Kingdom which lasted about five hundred years. During that time, people had developed own unique culture including folk music and dance.” He also plans to teach “’Oboro Zukiyo,’ which could be translated as ‘Misty Moon.’ It was composed in 1912, after the Meiji Restoration. Around that time, a lot of things came into Japan from Western countries, including classical music. Japanese composers incorporated Japanese folk with Western classical influences and composed some beautiful songs.”
events.title: Traditional Japanese Song Workshop (Portland Folkmusic Society)

events.summary: The Literary Arts Bookstore & Cafe is pleased to welcome author heidi restrepo rhodes to celebrate her debut short story collection, Ampersand Organ. About the book: A fearless, expansive collection that blurs the boundary between body and poem, wielding a liberatory lyric impulse that revels from neuron to nebula and back. Here is a book of many hearts, a revolutionary tide pool, a mycelial space and sensorium where our neural pathways are “always shared, collective, and entangled.” In this “more-than-human lyric,” heidi andrea restrepo rhodes offers the ampersand, a mode of encounter that unfixes the reader. This form—a lyric prose poem beginning, midsentence, with an ampersand—accesses the intimacies of a life shaped by perpetual “and-ing.” These ampersands move by associative leap, synesthetic braid, and inter-species blur to revel in everything that makes us more than singular subjects. Neuroqueering poetics, rhodes writes toward deft and loving excess: spillage, echolalia, stutter, loop, and non-linear detour, refiguring what the lyric can be and what the body can do. These poems revolt against all forms of supremacy, inviting us into unexpected kinship with animal, mineral, vegetal, and heavenly bodies, each replete with its own languages, temporalities, histories, and worlds. Tending an everyday eroticism with its “heart at the sleeve, in the palm,” Ampersand Organ is unafraid to feel, to feel again, to feel feeling wherever it’s wildly felt. Here is a radiant, divergent, emergent field guide for how we might all shiver and shimmer into the and and and . . .

Join Professor Palshikar, a New York-based, second generation Indian magician as he visits the region and Portland-based Historical Conjurer, Professor DR Schreiber for an unique evening of mystery and history. WORLD OF MAGIC: From Conjurer to Jadugar Thursday, August 13th, 2026 Doors open at 7pm Show at 8pm The Victorian Belle Mansion 1441 N. McClellan Street Portland, OR ADVANCED TICKETS: VIP Front Row Table Single Seat - $40.00 Second Row Table Single Seat - $35.00 Tall Bistro Table for 4 People - $140.00 General Admission Single Ticket - $25.00 Standing Room Ticket - $20.00 Ticket prices are for the show only and do not include food/drink. Tickets at: https://victorianbelle.com/shows-events/ About the performers: Professor Palshikar Shreeyash is the leading performer of world magic. Born in India thirteen days after Halloween, his ancestors include a Mormon prophet, Hindu priest, and an Indian magician. He has lived and worked around the world for decades, and is now based in New York. He began performing in school, and has traveled the world ever since. Combining the best of East & West, Shreeyash created fusion jadoo. Executives, college presidents, city mayors, and even royalty enjoy his fun, unique, bespoke performances and talks. Dr. Palshikar earned a PhD in South Asian studies from University of Chicago and has taught at Oxford, Yale, the School of Oriental and African Studies in London, and Fordham University in New York. He won a Fulbright fellowship to study traditional Indian magic with the last living performers, and has studied Chicago magic and improv. He has collaborated with the American Centers in Delhi, Mumbai and Kolkata, an Emmy award winning Broadway producer/director, New York based Bindlestiff Cirkus, the Asian Arts Initiative, WHYY, FirstPerson Arts, FringeArts, and others to share the wonder of Indian magic in venues around the world for 3 decades. He consulted on the Disney+ and Discovery series Beyond Belief, on a Vanishing Inc documentary, and is creating an original film on Indian magic. He has appeared on the Holland America World Cruises, at Harvard, Yale, and at the Smithsonian. Enjoy his fusion jadoo live, up close and in person: fun, enchanting, and enlightening. Audiences never forget it. Come, let him take a peek into your mind. Professor DR Schreiber The World of the Historical Conjurer Early in the 18th century, magic (or conjuring as it was referred) emerged as a genuine art form and entertainment. Professors of natural philosophy and conjuring would rent taverns, legitimate theaters or lecture halls for the exhibition and displays of legerdemain, necromancy, or what would today be called “illusion” and “magic tricks.” Top dollar would be paid by the citizens of Europe to see the latest discoveries in the science of “natural philosophy.” Today, Professor DR Schreiber presents an historic look at the beginnings of modern magic in his performances and exhibitions. Join Professor DR Schreiber as he leads you on a stroll through the past centuries of conjuring entertainment. His unique presentations entertain while educating the audience about historical events, literary and cultural figures, and the science and art of conjuring. Now you too can experience magic, as it was centuries ago. \------
events.title: WORLD OF MAGIC: From Conjurer to Jadugar

From veteran writer and activist Curtis White comes a concise yet potent guide to standing up to the myriad tyrannies of our current political landscape. We live in a time where independent thinking, love of literature and ideas, and passion for human expression are all under attack from a ruthless and uncaring government and a culture that values only immediate gratification and digital flash. In On Resistance \(Melville House\), White offers spiritual hope and intellectual fortification for those in despair about the bankruptcy of American life. Drawing on a range of books, films, essays, and artworks, White shows how our rich collective literary heritage gives us mental ammunition for our fight against the forces that would reduce us all to commodities and consumers. events.summary: Run Time: 175 min. TICKETS $25 Doors 6:30 p.m.; Conversation at 7 p.m.; Wild will screen after the conversation. Select Showtime to Purchase Tickets Click here to learn more about accessibility at the Tomorrow Theater. THE EXPERIENCE The state of Oregon is a magical place full of beautiful, diverse landscapes ranging from rugged ocean coastlines to rain-soaked temperate forests, arid high deserts and plains, fertile valleys, and volcanic mountain ranges, to name a few. Tonight we celebrate this majestic beauty by screening the 2014 film Wild, which was largely filmed in Oregon using the state's landscapes as stand-ins for other states' locations along the Pacific Coast Trail. Join us for a very special discussion with author Cheryl Strayed, whose memoir Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail inspired the feature film Wild; William L. Sullivan, author of 28 books and guides and hundreds of articles about the Pacific Northwest; and filmmaker Ime Etuk, whose feature Outdoor School follows a young urban teenager discovering peace and comfort in the natural splendor we call Oregon. This program is made possible with a grant from the America 250 Oregon Commission. Following the conversation, we will screen the film Wild, based on the 2012 memoir by Cheryl Strayed. ON SCREEN: Wild 2014. Directed by Jean-Marc Vallée. Runtime: 115 minutes. Rated R. Based on the 2012 memoir by Cheryl Strayed Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Coast Trail, Wild follows a woman with a tragic past who decides to start her new life by hiking for one thousand miles on the Pacific Crest Trail. Filmed largely in Oregon. ON STAGE: Cheryl Strayed \(Author\) - Cheryl Strayed is the author of the \#1 New York Times bestseller Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail, which was made into an Oscar-nominated film. Her bestselling collection of Dear Sugar columns, Tiny Beautiful Things, was adapted for a Hulu television show and as a play that continues to be staged in theaters nationwide. Strayed's other books are the critically acclaimed novel, Torch, and the bestselling collection Brave Enough, which brings together more than one hundred of her inspiring quotes. Her books have sold more than 5 million copies around the world and have been translated into forty languages. Her award-winning essays and short stories have been published in The Best American Essays, the New York Times, the Washington Post Magazine, Vogue, and elsewhere. Strayed is also a popular podcaster, having hosted the shows Sugar Calling and Dear Sugars, which she made with Steve Almond for the New York Times. She's now the host of the weekly podcast Mind Over Mountain for the iHeart Women's Sports network. She lives in Portland, Oregon. Photo credit Brian McDonnell. William L. Sullivan \(Author\) - William L. Sullivan is the author of 28 books and hundreds of articles about Oregon, including a weekly "Oregon Trails" column for Lookout: Eugene-Springfield . A fifth-generation Oregonian, Sullivan began hiking at the age of five and has been exploring new trails ever since. After studying at Deep Springs College in the California desert, receiving an English degree from Cornell University, and studying linguistics at Germany's Heidelberg University, he earned an M.A. in German literature from the University of Oregon. He has been happily married to the artist Janell Sorensen for more than 50 years. Sullivan's hobbies include backcountry ski touring, playing the pipe organ and harpsichord, reading foreign language novels, and promoting libraries. He co-chaired the campaign to build Eugene's downtown library, served on the Oregon State Library Board, and is president of the Lane Library League, a citizen group with the goal of extending library service to the 80,000 people in Lane County who currently lack service. Sullivan served for eight years on the board of the conservation group Oregon Wild and is a past president of the Round Table Club of Eugene. Sullivan organizes three author events each year-the Oregon Authors Table at the Art & the Vineyard Festival in Eugene on the 4th of July weekend, the Oregon Authors Table at the Oregon State Fair from late August through early September in Salem, and the Authors & Artists Fair, a fundraiser for the Lane Library League. Ime Etuk \(Filmmaker\) - Etuk believes the first step in storytelling is listening-deeply, openly, and without assumption. Whether writing, directing, or producing, he begins with rooting work in real stories and lived experiences. He aims to explore important emotional truths through fiction. His commitment is to honor communities and bring visibility to what's often overlooked or unheard. As a first-generation Nigerian raised in Portland, Etuk spent his life moving between cultural worlds-often translating himself in spaces that didn't fully see him. That sense of in-between shaped how he views identity, belonging, and transformation. It also drives the kinds of stories he tells: ones grounded in resilience, tension, and the quiet power of becoming. He is inspired by oral traditions, community histories, and the collective memory of those whose stories have too often been erased or ignored. His work draws on these influences and fuses them with his training in journalism, film, and theater. Over time, his practice has evolved from simply directing films to creating spaces for others to share their stories. He leads Lion Speaks, a nonprofit that mentors historically excluded Black and BIPOC creatives in media. Collaboration, mentorship, and access are central to his creative process. He often begins new work by listening: conducting interviews and gathering narratives that can be transformed into film, theater, or multimedia pieces. His goal is to build a body of work that is emotionally grounded and culturally expansive-films, series, and collaborative projects that foster reflection, empathy, and connection, while widening the circle of who gets to be seen and heard. His latest feature film, Outdoor School, premiered at the American Black Film Festival in 2025 and is currently on the festival circuit. Based on a true story, first shared on The Moth, and featured in the New York Times bestselling book, How to Tell a Story, the film explores themes of resilience, homelessness, and transformation in 1990's Portland.

Plus, they will unlock the jaw-dropping secrets of the incredible incognito, head-scratching band, Invisible Sex! events.summary: Surgery always carries some level of risk, and not every unexpected outcome is the result of negligence. However, when a healthcare professional fails to meet the accepted standard of medical care and that failure causes avoidable harm, the situation may amount to Surgical Negligence. Determining the difference often requires a careful review of medical records, expert opinions, and the circumstances surrounding the procedure. Warning signs can include operating on the wrong site, delayed treatment of complications, retained surgical instruments, anesthesia errors, or inadequate post-operative care. It is also important to consider whether the patient was properly informed of the risks before consenting to surgery. Establishing negligence involves proving that the injury was preventable and directly caused by substandard care rather than an unavoidable complication. Because these cases can be medically and legally complex, professional legal guidance is essential. Ciano Carroll Solicitors represents individuals who believe they have suffered avoidable harm due to medical errors and helps them understand whether they may have a valid claim. Their experience in handling complex medical negligence matters enables clients to navigate the legal process with confidence. By working with independent medical experts and thoroughly investigating each case, the firm evaluates whether the required legal standard for negligence has been met. Anyone concerned about the outcome of a surgical procedure should seek advice as early as possible to protect their legal rights. events.summary: Surgical negligence under Irish law occurs when a surgeon, hospital, or other healthcare professional fails to provide the standard of care that a reasonably competent medical practitioner would have delivered in similar circumstances, resulting in avoidable harm to a patient. This can include operating on the wrong site, causing preventable surgical injuries, failing to obtain informed consent, leaving surgical instruments inside the body, or providing inadequate post-operative care. Every case is assessed on its own facts, and proving Surgical Negligence generally requires evidence showing that the accepted standard of medical care was breached and that the breach directly caused the injury. Patients may experience additional medical treatment, prolonged recovery, financial losses, or long-term physical and emotional effects because of negligent surgical care. Irish law allows eligible patients to seek compensation where negligence can be established through appropriate medical and legal evidence. Understanding your legal rights early can make a significant difference in protecting your interests and preserving important evidence. Seeking advice from experienced legal professionals helps clarify whether the circumstances meet the legal threshold for Surgical Negligence. Ciano Carroll Solicitors focuses on representing clients in complex medical negligence claims and provides guidance throughout the legal process with a clear understanding of Irish medical negligence law. events.summary: Proving a Surgical Negligence claim requires strong, well-documented evidence that demonstrates how a healthcare provider failed to meet the accepted standard of care and caused avoidable harm. Diagnostic scans, laboratory results, surgical notes, consent forms, and hospital records can further support the claim. Witness statements from medical professionals or others involved in the patient's care may also strengthen the evidence. It is essential to show not only that an error occurred but also that the mistake directly resulted in physical, emotional, or financial damage. Documentation of ongoing treatment, rehabilitation, lost income, and future medical needs can help demonstrate the full impact of the injury. Every case is unique, making a thorough investigation critical before legal proceedings begin. events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) in Portland, Oregon will open two new exhibitions in its Front and Center Galleries this August. tende·r·eprisal // futu·re·prise, a group exhibition of bronze works created by multiple artists through a collaborative process led by elijah jamal asani, will be featured in the Front Gallery. In the Center Gallery, large-scale wood sculptures by Philip A. Robinson Jr. will be paired with functional and sculptural ceramic works by Swapna Mukhopadhyay. Both exhibitions run August 7–September 12, 2026, with a joint reception on Thursday, August 20, from 6 to 8 p.m. elijah jamal asani, a Nigerian-American artist, convened an intergenerational group of regional Black artists to create a collection of contemporary bronze artifacts. Their work was made in response to the historic theft of the Benin Bronzes. “Dating back to the 13th century, artists from the Kingdom of Benin, which is in modern-day southern Nigeria, cast bronze into sacred altar pieces and vessels of ancestral memory,” says asani. “However, in 1897, thousands of these bronze artifacts were looted by British forces.” They have yet to be repatriated. As an act of “selfdetermined restitution,” asani worked with other Black artists to create new bronzes. MAC is honored to exhibit eleven of these sculptures, created by Adriene Cruz, Midnite Seed Abioto, Intisar Abioto, Hanifah Abioto, Vaughn Kimmons, Turiya Raiah, Nyasiah Calixte, Lea Dry, Hannah Dry, Nawens Dry, and elijah jamal asani. Swapna Mukhopadhyay creates functional and sculptural porcelain works, all hand built. “The combination of aesthetics and functionality in handmade folk artifacts has always fascinated me,” she says. “My grandmother made traditional Bengali quilts (kanthas) and wove mats for sitting on the floor (asanas). I now realize how deeply I was influenced by watching her work.” Delicate drawn elements adorn many of her ceramic surfaces, and several recent works incorporate textiles and found objects. Mukhopadhyay describes her process as “improvising around what’s available,” informed by her longtime study of ethnomathematics. A retired PSU professor, she sees mathematics as inherent to creative practice and creative expression as integral to daily life across many cultures. Her ceramic pieces are often small in scale and characterized by what she calls their “putting togetherness.” Philip A. Robinson Jr. is a sculptor and conceptual artist whose work has been exhibited nationally and internationally. Working primarily in wood and metal, Robinson creates large-scale figurative and patterned works that explore memory, structure, and identity. “My practice examines structure as a living system—how materials carry memory, how patterns encode history, and how built environments shape identity,” he explains. “Whether in wood or steel, I am asking how structure holds memory—and how we locate ourselves within it.” The exhibition will include pieces from several bodies of work, including a 42” x 61” sculpture from Welcome In, which examines belonging, and several works from The House of Regina, which honor the legacy of his late mother, Dr. Regina Arnold. Robinson holds a BFA in Studio Art from Skidmore College and an MFA in Sculpture from the Mason Gross School of the Arts at Rutgers University. The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. The galleries are free and open to the public during these hours. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org

events.summary: PDX CONTEMPORARY ART is pleased to present our summer group show Mixed Flock: 30 Years, marking the celebration of the gallery’s thirtieth anniversary. Mixed Flock comes from the idea of different species of birds gathering together for a variety of reasons including safety, cooperation, and community. In talking with wildlife scientist Derek Craighead about mixed flocks, Craighead suggested humans underestimate the sociability of animals, that wild animals will gather to be social, for fun, and for company. That’s worthwhile! For thirty years, PDX artist’s have been a wonderful mixed flock with each artist having their own way of seeing the world and approaching their art-making. Now is an important time to highlight and strengthen mixed flocks. Our country is a mixed flock, the “melting pot”, where diverse peoples, cultures, and ways exist together and we are better for it. This show is a celebration of the gallery’s many and varied artists, supporters, and collectors who make up our flock. Mixed Flock: 30 Years features work from represented and invited artists including: Anna Gray + Ryan Wilson Pauslen, Nick Blosser, Iván Carmona, Marjorie Dial, Amjad Faur, Bean Finneran, Jacques Flechemueller, Ellen George, Johannes GiararVictoria Haven, Elizabeth Knight, Justin L’Amie, Alma Allen, James Lavadour, Terran Last Gun, Nathan William Lambdin, Nancy Lorenz, Kristen Miller, Wes Mills, Jeffry Mitchell, Megan Murphy, Jenene Nagy, Ido Radon, Georgina Reskala, Joe Rudko, Tad Savinar, Susan Seubert, Adam Sorensen, Barbara Stafford, Storm Tharp, Gus Van Sant, Nell Warren, Heather Watkins, Marie Watt, and Yamamoto Masao.
events.title: Mixed Flock: 30 Years

Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Chefas Projects is delighted to welcome back sculptor Jessie Weitzel Le Grand for her fourth exhibition with the gallery entitled Astral Accessories. Communication arrives fractured: as static, interference, intuition, and half-remembered technologies that once promised connection. In Astral Accessories, Portland-based artist Jessie Weitzel Le Grand presents a new body of sculptural work that imagines obsolete technological devices as enigmatic relics from alternate realities. Equal parts artifact, machine, and living organism, the sculptures transform familiar forms into mysterious conduits for uncertainty, speculation, and wonder. Drawing on the visual language of outdated communications technology, the exhibition considers what remains when systems of transmission fail or become obsolete. Unmanageable and invisible, signals continue to pass through space, whirring beyond perception, like sirens too quiet to hear. Meaning emerges imperfectly through noise, distortion, and interruption, where messages are received as static, interference, and fragmented memory rather than clear transmission. Rather than offering resolution, Astral Accessories embraces ambiguity. The works suggest speculative tools for communicating across impossible distances: between worlds, across time, or with forms of intelligence that remain just beyond comprehension. Suspended between archaeology and science fiction, the sculptures ask viewers to reconsider the objects that mediate our relationships with technology, memory, and the unknown. Utilizing an eclectic array of materials, including ceramics, thermoplastic, flashe paint, and even materials used in fly tying, Weitzel Le Grand blurs the boundaries between art, artifact, and technology. Interested in exploring how we perceive reality and questioning the certainty of what we see, she embeds natural elements such as orchids, moths, and fragments of coral within computer motherboards, rotary telephones, and other obsolete technologies in disorienting, exuberant configurations. By reimagining these nostalgic devices in playful yet unfamiliar ways, she encourages viewers to question their function and invent their own narratives around the mysterious systems they seem to inhabit. By transforming obsolete technologies into uncanny relics, Weitzel Le Grand creates a landscape where the familiar becomes strange and failed technologies become vessels for new forms of connection. Jessie Weitzel Le Grand (b. 1987) was born and raised in Portland, Oregon, where she continues to live and work. She received a BFA from the Pacific Northwest College of Art and an MAT from Marylhurst University. Her work has recently been exhibited at Galerie Lefebvre & Fils (Paris, France), Outback Arthouse (Los Angeles, California), Oregon Contemporary (Portland, Oregon), and as part of Lazy Oaf's Take A Break exhibition (London, United Kingdom). She is the co-founder of carnation Contemporary, a collective of emerging and mid-career artists from the Pacific Northwest championing critical contemporary art, and Well Well Projects, an artist-member gallery in Portland's Kenton neighborhood. In 2025, she was featured in Create! Magazine Issue #49 and is currently represented by Chefas Projects.
events.title: JESSIE WEITZEL LE GRAND | ASTRAL ACCESSORIES

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Where Do Geese Fly at Night?, San Francisco–based artist Lindsay Stripling's debut solo exhibition with the gallery. Through luminous watercolor paintings, Stripling creates dreamlike worlds where memory, intuition, and the rhythms of the natural world converge. Her imagined landscapes and nature-infused portraits blur the boundaries between observation and imagination, inviting viewers into spaces where storytelling becomes a means of navigating identity, belonging, and transformation. Rooted in experimentation, texture, and play, Stripling's practice embraces watercolor as both a precise and unpredictable medium. Layers of transparent color accumulate into richly atmospheric compositions that evoke fleeting memories, quiet psychological states, and the mysterious logic of dreams. Plants, animals, and human figures coexist in environments that feel at once deeply familiar and gently surreal, suggesting a world in which the human experience is inseparable from the more-than-human landscape. Throughout Where Do Geese Fly at Night?, Stripling explores themes of nature, time, community, psychology, and personal mythology. Rather than offering fixed narratives, her paintings unfold as open-ended visual poems, encouraging viewers to project their own memories and emotional landscapes into the work. Each composition balances meticulous craftsmanship with a spirit of curiosity, revealing beauty in uncertainty and wonder in the everyday. The exhibition's title poses a deceptively simple question, one that gestures toward the unseen journeys taking place beyond the limits of perception. Like migratory paths traced through darkness, Stripling's paintings invite contemplation of the invisible forces that shape our relationships with ourselves, one another, and the natural world. Lindsay Stripling is a San Francisco–based painter, illustrator, and educator. Working primarily in watercolor, she explores the intersections of storytelling, memory, dreams, and ecology through richly layered paintings that combine intimate portraiture with expansive natural imagery. events.summary: This summer, a multi-sensory art experience called Shifting Realities will take over Porsche Studio Portland for a creative journey produced by artists from Portland and across the country. The space turns into a living canvas where you don’t just observe the work, you become part of it. Across multiple interactive environments, you’ll see sound take physical form, design in real time using light and gesture, and step into spaces that respond to your movement, energy, and input. From large-scale visual installations to hands-on creative moments and a multisensory tasting experience, each part of the experience is designed to blur the line between artist and audience. Guests move through the experience in timed groups, progressing together through each space while still having room to explore and interact along the way. Running June 4 through August 31, Shifting Realities is a 100 minute limited-run installation that’s built for all ages and occasions. Tickets start at $39 ($41.34 incl. fees), with reduced pricing for kids and options for VIP, private, and group bookings.

events.summary: Instructor | Tickets | Series Schedule | Parking Enjoy a blossom-filled afternoon at the beautiful Lan Su Chinese Garden with the return of Steep & Paint. With all materials provided and admission included, all you need to bring is yourself! We’re bringing this series back by popular demand and newly reimagined in partnership with the Oregon Botanical Artists \(OBA\). This immersive afternoon experience invites you to slow down, look closely, and connect with plants through tea, conversation, and hands-on art-making. Our August 14 Lotus session with Zebith Thalden will use colored pencils as the medium. Each session weaves together horticulture, tea culture, and botanical art in a relaxed, welcoming setting: Learn the plant up close: A Lan Su gardener leads a close-up botanical show-and-tell, sharing seasonal plant facts, cultural stories, and growing insights. Taste the season: Enjoy a sampling of seasonal teas from Yun Shui Teahouse. Create botanical art: An OBA artist guides a full botanical art class inspired by the featured plant. Whether you’re returning to Steep & Paint or joining for the first time, this refreshed program offers an even richer way to experience Lan Su. Bring a friend with you and let’s Steep & Paint together! Meet the Instructor: Zebith Thalden “Spice Bush or Western Sweetshrub \(Calycanthus occidentalis\)” by Zebith Thalden Zebith Thalden is a US-based studio artist, author, and instructor. Her artwork has been featured in galleries, cultural centers, and art museums, including the CICA Museum in Gimpo-si, South Korea; the Academy of Science in Canberra, Australia; American Association for the Advancement of Science in Washington DC; and the Annmarie Sculpture Garden in Dowell, Maryland. She has been in residence at Zion National Park and PLAYA: Center for the Intersection of Art and Science. She has also been a featured speaker at Portland State College of the Arts: School of Art \+ Design, Red Butte Garden and Arboretum, and Southern Utah University. Her book The Insect Artist: How to Observe, Draw, and Paint Butterflies, Bees, and More was released by Timber Press on March 12, 2024. She received an MFA from Goddard College and a BFA from the Rhode Island School of Design. Meet Our Partner: Oregon Botanical Artists \(OBA\) Oregon Botanical Artists is a nonprofit organization dedicated to promoting contemporary botanical art while honoring its long-standing traditions. Founded in 2012, the organization supports a diverse community of artists who celebrate the beauty and diversity of plant life through detailed and scientifically informed artwork. Oregon Botanical Artists is affiliated with the American Society of Botanical Artists as an Artists Circle. Instructor | Tickets | Series Schedule | Parking Steep & Paint Need to Know Each class session is independent — participants are welcome to register for any individual class without attending others. Registration fee includes full-day admission to Lan Su Chinese Garden. Get Tickets Lan Su Members & Guests: $56.95 General: $66.95 Note: A $0.95 service fee is reflected in each paid ticket Full Series Schedule Set a new monthly Friday tradition, or treat someone special to an amazing afternoon of creativity! Parking & Directions Free Lan Su Parking There is free first come, first served parking in our sister lot next to the garden at 424 NW Third Avenue. Additional metered parking and garages are available on surrounding streets.

events.summary: TICKETS truewest.info/GWDR-26 On Sale Friday, May 15 at 10am PT This Event is All Ages ---------------------------------------- Gillian Welch and David Rawlings are pillars of the modern acoustic music world and their rich and remarkable careers span over twenty-five years. They have been hailed by Pitchfork as “modern masters of American folk” and “protectors of the American folk song” by Rolling Stone and the New York Times says “their combined voices operate beyond simple sonic harmony. There are emotional inquiries at play. If Welch’s voice delivers the good news or the hard news of the world, Rawlings’s voice comes underneath, asking how much deeper the sadness can go or what fresh heights the ecstatic can climb to.” Their most recent 10th studio album, Woodland, won the 2025 Best Folk Album GRAMMY. Woodland was named for and recorded at Welch and Rawlings’ own Woodland Sound Studios in Nashville, TN. Of the album and studio, Welch said, “Woodland is at the heart of everything we do and has been for the last twenty some years. The past four years were spent almost entirely within its walls, bringing it back to life after the 2020 tornado and making this record. The music is \(songs are\) a swirl of contradictions, emptiness, fullness, joy, grief, destruction, permanence. Now.” The new 10-song collection mingles full band tracks with intricate duet performances all tied together with the duo’s signature sound and lyricism and cements the pair’s iconoclastic position at the forefront of acoustic music. After moving to Nashville in the 1990s, Welch was launched into the public consciousness when Emmylou Harris recorded a cover of Welch’s “Orphan Girl.” Her career continued to flourish as her 1996 debut Revival, produced by T Bone Burnett, was released to critical acclaim. Firmly on the roots music map following the release, Welch and Rawlings followed up that GRAMMY nominated album release with 1998’s Hell Among The Yearlings, a stark duet record that further solidified the duo as a force in the folk music scene

What initially seems like a mere publicity stunt soon becomes a soul-baring battle of wills. Only one can win, but for all involved, the truck holds the key to their own private American dream. The mix of people in this contest includes: an unlikeable prior winner who is a bit racist; the son of an immigrant who wants to be a veterinarian; a USMC veteran; an older woman (with her husband for support) who really needs the money; a Texas evangelical; a beauty queen; an older man (and his wife as support) who is recovering from a fall from a big rig; and a few other folks. events.summary: Medical experts play a crucial role in evaluating injuries that occur during assisted childbirth by carefully reviewing medical records, delivery notes, imaging scans, and the condition of both the mother and baby. They assess whether forceps, vacuum extraction, or other assisted delivery methods were used appropriately according to accepted medical standards. Specialists also examine the timing of interventions, fetal monitoring records, and whether alternative delivery options should have been considered. Their findings help determine if the injuries resulted from unavoidable complications or preventable medical negligence. In cases involving Traume from Instrumental Delivery, experts evaluate the extent of physical and neurological harm, the expected long-term impact, and the treatment or rehabilitation that may be required. They may consult with obstetricians, pediatric neurologists, radiologists, and rehabilitation professionals to provide an objective medical opinion. This expert evidence is often essential in establishing whether the standard of care fell below what would reasonably be expected. A detailed medical assessment can also help quantify the financial and personal impact of the injury, including ongoing healthcare needs and loss of quality of life. Families seeking answers often rely on experienced legal professionals to interpret these findings within the context of a compensation claim. Ciano Carroll Solicitors focuses on complex medical negligence cases, including those involving assisted childbirth injuries, and works closely with independent medical experts to build well-supported claims. By combining detailed medical evidence with legal expertise, the firm helps clients understand their rights and pursue fair compensation where negligence has contributed to avoidable birth injuries.
events.title: How do medical experts assess injuries caused by assisted childbirth?

events.summary: Surgery always carries some level of risk, and not every unexpected outcome is the result of negligence. However, when a healthcare professional fails to meet the accepted standard of medical care and that failure causes avoidable harm, the situation may amount to Surgical Negligence. Determining the difference often requires a careful review of medical records, expert opinions, and the circumstances surrounding the procedure. Warning signs can include operating on the wrong site, delayed treatment of complications, retained surgical instruments, anesthesia errors, or inadequate post-operative care. It is also important to consider whether the patient was properly informed of the risks before consenting to surgery. Establishing negligence involves proving that the injury was preventable and directly caused by substandard care rather than an unavoidable complication. Because these cases can be medically and legally complex, professional legal guidance is essential. Ciano Carroll Solicitors represents individuals who believe they have suffered avoidable harm due to medical errors and helps them understand whether they may have a valid claim. Their experience in handling complex medical negligence matters enables clients to navigate the legal process with confidence. By working with independent medical experts and thoroughly investigating each case, the firm evaluates whether the required legal standard for negligence has been met. Anyone concerned about the outcome of a surgical procedure should seek advice as early as possible to protect their legal rights. Understanding the distinction between an accepted surgical risk and Surgical Negligence is the first step toward determining whether compensation may be available.
events.title: How can you tell if a surgical complication was actually negligence?

events.summary: Instrumental delivery can be a necessary medical intervention during childbirth, but when forceps or a vacuum extractor are used incorrectly, mothers may suffer serious physical and emotional harm. Injuries such as severe perineal tears, pelvic floor damage, nerve injuries, excessive bleeding, or long-term pain can have lasting effects on daily life. If these injuries resulted from avoidable medical errors or substandard care, the affected mother may have grounds to pursue a compensation claim. Establishing negligence typically requires evidence that healthcare professionals failed to meet the accepted standard of care and that this directly caused the injury. Every case is unique, so medical records, expert opinions, and the circumstances surrounding the delivery are carefully evaluated. Claims can help recover compensation for medical expenses, rehabilitation, lost income, ongoing care, and pain and suffering. The physical and emotional Traume from Instrumental Delivery may also be considered when assessing the full impact of the injury on the mother's quality of life. Understanding your legal rights is an important first step toward seeking justice. Ciano Carroll Solicitors focuses on complex medical negligence claims and provides guidance to individuals who believe their injuries were caused by negligent medical treatment. Their experience in investigating childbirth-related negligence helps clients understand whether they have a valid claim and what legal options may be available. Parents should also request copies of medical records, including labour, delivery, and neonatal care notes, as these documents may help clarify what happened during childbirth. It is often beneficial to keep a detailed record of symptoms, treatments, and conversations with healthcare providers. In some situations, concerns may arise about Traume from Instrumental Delivery, particularly if forceps or a vacuum extractor were used during a difficult birth and the child later developed injuries. While not every complication is the result of negligence, a thorough legal review can determine whether accepted medical standards were followed. Understanding the cause of a birth injury can help families make informed decisions about their next steps. events.summary: Proving a Surgical Negligence claim requires strong, well-documented evidence that demonstrates how a healthcare provider failed to meet the accepted standard of care and caused avoidable harm. Medical records are often the foundation of the case, providing a detailed timeline of diagnosis, treatment, surgery, and follow-up care. Expert medical opinions are equally important because they help establish whether the surgeon's actions fell below the standard expected of a reasonably competent professional. Diagnostic scans, laboratory results, surgical notes, consent forms, and hospital records can further support the claim. Witness statements from medical professionals or others involved in the patient's care may also strengthen the evidence. It is essential to show not only that an error occurred but also that the mistake directly resulted in physical, emotional, or financial damage. Documentation of ongoing treatment, rehabilitation, lost income, and future medical needs can help demonstrate the full impact of the injury. Every case is unique, making a thorough investigation critical before legal proceedings begin. An experienced solicitor can identify the evidence needed, obtain independent expert reports, and build a compelling legal argument. A well-prepared case supported by credible evidence significantly improves the likelihood of achieving a fair outcome.

events.summary: Surgical negligence under Irish law occurs when a surgeon, hospital, or other healthcare professional fails to provide the standard of care that a reasonably competent medical practitioner would have delivered in similar circumstances, resulting in avoidable harm to a patient. This can include operating on the wrong site, causing preventable surgical injuries, failing to obtain informed consent, leaving surgical instruments inside the body, or providing inadequate post-operative care. Every case is assessed on its own facts, and proving Surgical Negligence generally requires evidence showing that the accepted standard of medical care was breached and that the breach directly caused the injury. Patients may experience additional medical treatment, prolonged recovery, financial losses, or long-term physical and emotional effects because of negligent surgical care. Irish law allows eligible patients to seek compensation where negligence can be established through appropriate medical and legal evidence. Understanding your legal rights early can make a significant difference in protecting your interests and preserving important evidence. Seeking advice from experienced legal professionals helps clarify whether the circumstances meet the legal threshold for Surgical Negligence. Ciano Carroll Solicitors focuses on representing clients in complex medical negligence claims and provides guidance throughout the legal process with a clear understanding of Irish medical negligence law. Their experience in handling surgical negligence cases helps clients understand the evidence required, the claims process, and the potential outcomes. Whether the issue involves a surgical error, delayed treatment after surgery, or another avoidable complication, obtaining informed legal advice is an important first step toward pursuing justice and fair compensation.

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) in Portland, Oregon will open two new exhibitions in its Front and Center Galleries this August. tende·r·eprisal // futu·re·prise, a group exhibition of bronze works created by multiple artists through a collaborative process led by elijah jamal asani, will be featured in the Front Gallery. In the Center Gallery, large-scale wood sculptures by Philip A. Robinson Jr. will be paired with functional and sculptural ceramic works by Swapna Mukhopadhyay. Both exhibitions run August 7–September 12, 2026, with a joint reception on Thursday, August 20, from 6 to 8 p.m. elijah jamal asani, a Nigerian-American artist, convened an intergenerational group of regional Black artists to create a collection of contemporary bronze artifacts. Their work was made in response to the historic theft of the Benin Bronzes. “Dating back to the 13th century, artists from the Kingdom of Benin, which is in modern-day southern Nigeria, cast bronze into sacred altar pieces and vessels of ancestral memory,” says asani. “However, in 1897, thousands of these bronze artifacts were looted by British forces.” They have yet to be repatriated. As an act of “selfdetermined restitution,” asani worked with other Black artists to create new bronzes. MAC is honored to exhibit eleven of these sculptures, created by Adriene Cruz, Midnite Seed Abioto, Intisar Abioto, Hanifah Abioto, Vaughn Kimmons, Turiya Raiah, Nyasiah Calixte, Lea Dry, Hannah Dry, Nawens Dry, and elijah jamal asani. Swapna Mukhopadhyay creates functional and sculptural porcelain works, all hand built. “The combination of aesthetics and functionality in handmade folk artifacts has always fascinated me,” she says. “My grandmother made traditional Bengali quilts (kanthas) and wove mats for sitting on the floor (asanas). I now realize how deeply I was influenced by watching her work.” Delicate drawn elements adorn many of her ceramic surfaces, and several recent works incorporate textiles and found objects. Mukhopadhyay describes her process as “improvising around what’s available,” informed by her longtime study of ethnomathematics. A retired PSU professor, she sees mathematics as inherent to creative practice and creative expression as integral to daily life across many cultures. Her ceramic pieces are often small in scale and characterized by what she calls their “putting togetherness.” Philip A. Robinson Jr. is a sculptor and conceptual artist whose work has been exhibited nationally and internationally. Working primarily in wood and metal, Robinson creates large-scale figurative and patterned works that explore memory, structure, and identity. “My practice examines structure as a living system—how materials carry memory, how patterns encode history, and how built environments shape identity,” he explains. “Whether in wood or steel, I am asking how structure holds memory—and how we locate ourselves within it.” The exhibition will include pieces from several bodies of work, including a 42” x 61” sculpture from Welcome In, which examines belonging, and several works from The House of Regina, which honor the legacy of his late mother, Dr. Regina Arnold. Robinson holds a BFA in Studio Art from Skidmore College and an MFA in Sculpture from the Mason Gross School of the Arts at Rutgers University. The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. The galleries are free and open to the public during these hours. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org

events.summary: PDX CONTEMPORARY ART is pleased to present our summer group show Mixed Flock: 30 Years, marking the celebration of the gallery’s thirtieth anniversary. Mixed Flock comes from the idea of different species of birds gathering together for a variety of reasons including safety, cooperation, and community. In talking with wildlife scientist Derek Craighead about mixed flocks, Craighead suggested humans underestimate the sociability of animals, that wild animals will gather to be social, for fun, and for company. That’s worthwhile! For thirty years, PDX artist’s have been a wonderful mixed flock with each artist having their own way of seeing the world and approaching their art-making. Now is an important time to highlight and strengthen mixed flocks. Our country is a mixed flock, the “melting pot”, where diverse peoples, cultures, and ways exist together and we are better for it. This show is a celebration of the gallery’s many and varied artists, supporters, and collectors who make up our flock. Mixed Flock: 30 Years features work from represented and invited artists including: Anna Gray + Ryan Wilson Pauslen, Nick Blosser, Iván Carmona, Marjorie Dial, Amjad Faur, Bean Finneran, Jacques Flechemueller, Ellen George, Johannes GiararVictoria Haven, Elizabeth Knight, Justin L’Amie, Alma Allen, James Lavadour, Terran Last Gun, Nathan William Lambdin, Nancy Lorenz, Kristen Miller, Wes Mills, Jeffry Mitchell, Megan Murphy, Jenene Nagy, Ido Radon, Georgina Reskala, Joe Rudko, Tad Savinar, Susan Seubert, Adam Sorensen, Barbara Stafford, Storm Tharp, Gus Van Sant, Nell Warren, Heather Watkins, Marie Watt, and Yamamoto Masao.

Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

Botanical Alchemy Experience the alchemical marriage of Mary Lyn Gough’s earthen floral watercolors and Kirra Teal Hellfritsch’s metamorphic jewelry. Together, their work explores the transformation of the natural world through elemental materials and traditional craftsmanship. Rooted in botanical forms and natural processes, both artists celebrate the enduring beauty found within growth, decay, and renewal. Their work reveals the quiet magic of nature translated through paint and metal.
